key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the detention order was based on multiple grounds, including various acts of the appellant involving Hawala payments, searches and seizures of currency and documents, and statements from various individuals.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their statements and the details provided formed part of the grounds for detention, and that the detaining authority considered these statements in forming its opinion.

legal_representation.accused: Vikram Chaudhri, Sr. Adv., Sangram S. Saron, Harshit Sethi, Manish Verma, Rishi Sehgal, Ms. Pragati Sharma, Nikhil Jain, Advs.
legal_representation.state: Ms. Madhavi Divan, Ms. Binu Tamta, Ms. Ranjana Narayan, S. Wasim A. Qadri, Ms. Nidhi Khanna, B. Krishna Prasad, Advs.

investigation_status: Detention order passed under Section 3(1) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974; searches conducted, documents seized, statements recorded

appeal_history.trial_court: Writ petition dismissed as withdrawn with liberty to avail legal remedies

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the detention order was based on multiple grounds, and even if one ground was found to be non-existing or legally unsustainable, the detention order would still be valid under the principle of segregation of grounds in Section 5A of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the detention order was based on only one ground, and the various instances mentioned in the Grounds of Detention were merely subsidiary facts or further particulars of that single ground, thus making the principle of segregation in Section 5A inapplicable.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that if a detention order is based on more than one independent ground, it will still be valid even if one of the grounds is found to be non-existing or legally unsustainable, invoking the principle of segregation contained in Section 5A of the Act.
precedent_relied_upon: A. Sowkath Ali v. Union of India & Ors. (2000) 7 SCC 148; Vashisht Narain Karwaria v. State of U.P. & Anr. (1990) 2 SCC 629; Vakil Singh v. State of J. & K. & Anr. (1975) 3 SCC 545; Khudiram Das v. The State of West Bengal & Ors. (1975) 2 SCC 81; Madan Lal Anand v. Union of India & Ors. (1990) 1 SCC 81; Prakash Chandra Mehta v. Commissioner and Secretary, Government of Kerala & Ors. (1985) Supp. SCC 144; Attorney General for India & Ors. v. Amratla/ Prajivandas & Ors. (1994) 5 SCC 54
